Newborn individuals of Speckled ray enter the world at a total length of 10.6 cm [Lb = 10.6 cm], a modest size that reflects an extended period of yolk-dependent development within the egg case. The incubation period for this species, sustained at a stable temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], lasts approximately 137 days [ab = approximately 137 days], during which the embryo undergoes complete organogenesis before emerging as a fully formed benthic juvenile. This relatively lengthy gestation within the egg case is typical of many rajiform elasmobranchs and is thought to confer enhanced locomotor and foraging capabilities upon hatching. Upon emergence, the young ray immediately assumes a demersal lifestyle, preying upon small crustaceans and polychaetes in shallow coastal habitats. The initial body size at birth suggests a trade-off between maternal investment in yolk provisioning and the number of offspring produced per reproductive cycle, with larger egg cases yielding more developed neonates that face reduced predation risk during the first weeks of independent life. Field surveys in the Mediterranean have documented these dimensions consistently across several localities.

Growth proceeds steadily during the juvenile phase, with individuals eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] when fully grown. This asymptotic dimension is achieved after several years of continuous somatic expansion, during which the growing rays exploit increasingly larger benthic prey items. The maximum recorded adult wet weight corresponding to this length is approximately 1270 grams [Wwi = approximately 1270 grams], a value derived from length–weight regressions obtained from trawl survey specimens. The body mass at ultimate size places the Speckled ray among the medium-sized members of its genus, with a somewhat robust body plan that facilitates foraging on hard-shelled invertebrates. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that Rajidae attaining a similar maximum length often exhibit weight values within the same order of magnitude, although local variation in prey availability and benthic productivity can influence the observed condition factor. Adults in the central Mediterranean tend to approach this maximum size more closely than those from the Adriatic, possibly due to differences in thermal regime and food abundance, though the ultimate length remains a fixed species-level trait.

Sexual maturation in Speckled ray occurs at a total length of 50.6 cm [Lp = 50.6 cm] when considering both sexes pooled, although a notable sexual dimorphism exists in the timing of puberty. Males become reproductively mature at a smaller size, specifically at a total length of 48.8 cm [Lp = 48.8 cm], while females require a slightly larger body dimension before initiating gonadal recrudescence. This pattern of earlier male maturation is widespread among elasmobranchs and is generally interpreted as a consequence of differential energetic demands, with females needing to attain a larger body size to accommodate yolk production and egg case formation. Upon reaching these threshold lengths, the claspers of males become fully calcified and the ovaries of females begin to produce vitellogenic follicles. The onset of reproductive activity is therefore tightly linked to somatic growth rather than to a fixed chronological age, a strategy that buffers the population against interannual variability in food supply. The values reported here were obtained from histological examination of captured specimens.

Reproductive output in this species, when measured under the stable thermal conditions of the Mediterranean at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], is characterized by a maximum rate of egg production. Females are capable of laying 1 egg per egg case [N_R_i = 1 egg per egg case] and producing between 20 and 62 egg cases per year [Ri = between 20 and 62 egg cases per year], an annual fecundity that places the Speckled ray among the more prolific members of the Rajidae. This output is achieved through the repeated deposition of individual egg cases, each containing a single fertilized ovum, over an extended breeding season that spans several months. The annual reproductive investment is considerable given the large size of the egg cases relative to the female body, and it imposes significant energetic costs that are reflected in the seasonal decline in maternal body condition. The production of up to 62 egg cases in a single year likely represents an upper physiological limit attained only by the largest females under optimal prey conditions, whereas smaller or younger breeders typically contribute fewer capsules to the population. Each egg case is deposited on sandy or muddy substrates, where it remains anchored by horn-like projections until the embryo completes its development.

The overall life history of Speckled ray is characterized by a maximum lifespan estimated at 15 years [am = 15 years] when maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], a longevity that is consistent with the slow pace of life typical of many benthic elasmobranchs. This extended lifespan allows females to accumulate multiple reproductive bouts over their lifetime, which is essential for population persistence given the moderate annual fecundity and the relatively advanced age at first reproduction. The combination of a long juvenile period, delayed sexual maturation, and iteroparous reproduction aligns with the classical K-selected life history strategy observed in most rajiform rays. Natural mortality in older individuals is thought to result from senescence of the reproductive organs and a gradual decline in foraging efficiency, although predation by larger elasmobranchs and marine mammals also contributes to adult mortality in some regions. The species shows little evidence of reproductive senescence, with females continuing to produce viable egg cases up to the final years of life. Comparative analyses within the genus Raja suggest that the 15-year lifespan is near the upper end of the range for medium-sized Mediterranean rays.
